LEARNING PATH LESSON · ANIMALS & SOUNDS · AGES 2 YEARS

Snake — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the longest out-breath in the deck: a hiss that stretches, a floor wiggle to match, and the one clear rule about real snakes.

What is this?

A snake is a long, legless animal with no sound except sssss — more air than voice, which makes it the change of pace after all the roaring cards.

What does it mean?

Sustained ssss is mouth-muscle and breath training in one: the same control later needed for blowing bubbles, blowing candles and saying long words clearly.

What does the child need to know?

Real snakes are a hands-off animal in every country there is. The card lets your toddler enjoy snakes safely, and the rule gets said the same simple way on every walk.

Why this matters

After the loud cards, a hiss resets the room. Parents discover quickly that a long sssss on the walk home is also a remarkably effective quieting spell.

What it teaches

Breath extension, tongue-tip control, whole-body wiggling imitation, and first rule-following about live creatures.

Words to learn

snakehisslongwiggleslowquiet

Say this to your child

“"A snake! Ssssssss. Can you hiss? Long and slow, like air coming out. Wiggle, wiggle — snakes slide on their tummies. Real snakes: we look, we never touch."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card and say snake, then hiss — sssssss — as long as your breath lasts.
  2. Wiggle together: lie on the floor, arms close, and slither along the rug making the hiss travel with you.
  3. Hunt snakes in books and drawers — belts and ribbons make fine pretend snakes for a careful wiggly parade.
  4. When the hiss comes out as a hissy giggle or a short ss!, stretch yours longer and see if they copy; length grows with practice, not pressure.
  5. Hiss at calm moments this week — the walk home, the bath fill-up — and say the real-snake rule once each time snakes come up.

Look closer at the picture

The card shows a snake hissing. Find the snake, find the sssss, then ask what shape the snake makes — long and curly is the answer the card draws.

Ask your child

"Where is the snake?" "What does the snake say?" "Can you hiss longer than me?" "Can you wiggle like a snake?"

What your child can say or do

A stretched "sssss" with the tongue poking out, or a short hiss and a triumphant floor-flop. Some toddlers hiss at the kettle’s steam — a good moment to add hot, not a snake.

Out in the real world

Gardens, zoos and books hold real snakes; ribbons and belts hold the pretend ones. If snakes live near you, the rule travels on every walk — same words, same calm voice.

Try it together

Snake parade: hold a ribbon each, wiggle it along the floor to a slow hiss, then coil it up in a circle at the end — snakes rest coiled, and so does the game.

Understanding check

Ask what the snake says. An s-shaped hiss passes. Then watch for the wiggle at unexpected moments — a rug-slither during tidying-up means the snake lives here now.

Parent tips

Longer hisses come from longer out-breaths, so practise on the floor where bellies can feel the air move. Keep the real-snake rule to one sentence; simplicity is what makes rules stick at two.

Staying safe

Real snakes are look-never-touch, always — if you meet one, pick your toddler up, step back together, and save the hiss for the safety of the buggy ride home.

This lesson pairs with the Snake flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Animals & Sounds (Toddler 5).
